Cluster 03 Drill, Gene and Chromosomal Mutations, Molecular Techniques and Bioethics

H2 Biology 9477 · Book 2 · 9 questions · 148 marks · cumulative over Cluster 1 + Cluster 2 + Cluster 3 + Book 1

Answers sit directly under each part, hidden. Click Show answer only after you have said your full reasoning aloud for that part. Check (a) before you start (b) - that is the point of the layout.

Every stem is one or two sentences and every answer is long. No stem lists the axes to compare on, no stem tells you which option is wrong, and no stem contains its own answer. There is no multiple choice this time; every part is open. Nine of the eighteen parts carry the real figure from the paper it came from, not a redrawing.

Cumulative. Seven parts need an earlier cluster said cold - Q1(a) the reading frame, degeneracy and the stop codon from Cluster 2; Q3(a) the whole replication enzyme roster from Cluster 1, because PCR is defined here by what it does not use; Q4(a) the sugar-phosphate backbone and why the phosphates are negative; Q5(b) hydrogen bonding and melting temperature; Q6(b) enhancers and silencers acting at a distance; Q7(a) the centromere and the kinetochore; Q9 the transcriptional level of control. Four parts need Book 1 cold - Q1(a) primary structure deciding tertiary conformation, Q2(a) haemoglobin as the worked quaternary-structure example, Q3(b) what makes an enzyme thermostable and what an optimum temperature is, and Q4(b) the difference between a charged R group and a non-polar one. A Cluster 1 or Book 1 gap surfacing here is worth more than a clean Cluster 3 answer, so say it out loud when it happens.

What the marks reward, and it is not what Cluster 2 rewarded. Every mutation chain starts at the gene - a scheme in this Book rejects the first two marking points outright if the answer never mentions the DNA. Every technique step carries its purpose, because procedure alone scores nothing. And the lexicon is strict: aneuploidy not "Down syndrome" when naming the consequence of non-disjunction, non-homologous in the translocation definition, Taq polymerase not "a heat-stable polymerase", anode, constant charge density, and glutamate to valine with hydrophilic and hydrophobic attached to each.

Three traps here carry measured failure rates from real examiner reports: the meiosis I against meiosis II deduction in Q7(a), where the nearest published equivalent was answered correctly by only 45.66% of the cohort; the DNA-against-RNA primer point inside Q3(a), at 54.60%; and the expression-profile reading in Q9(a), which the examiner recorded as poorly done because candidates read the bands and then stopped without naming a regulatory cause.

A third of the raw question bank for this cluster is cut content, and none of it appears here. Restriction enzyme recognition sequences, sticky against blunt ends, restriction mapping and RFLP, cloning vectors and plasmids, ligation, insertional inactivation, transformation, gene therapy, DNA sequencing and profiling, Northern blotting and FISH mechanism are all absent from the 9477 syllabus. Questions
Q1 Q2 Q3 Q4 Q5 Q6 Q7 Q8 Q9

Question 1 [16 marks]

(a) Two patients each carry a change at the twelfth codon of the same 400-codon gene: in one it is a single-base substitution, in the other a single-base insertion. Predict which patient is more likely to have a working protein, and account for the difference. (answer in terms of the reading frame) [12]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Which of a single-base substitution and a single-base insertion is more likely to leave a working protein. [12]

1. The substitution is the more likely of the two to leave a working protein, because a substitution replaces one nucleotide pair with another and so changes at most one codon and at most one amino acid, whereas an insertion of one base changes every codon after it.

The four outcomes of the substitution, max 5:

2. Silent, the codon is changed, but the same amino acid is inserted into the protein because of the degeneracy of the genetic code, so the amino acid sequence is unchanged, there is no change in conformation and the function is not altered. There are 64 codons for 20 amino acids and the redundancy sits mostly at the third base of the codon, so a change at the third position very often gives a synonymous codon. [CROSS-CLUSTER: Cluster 2, and note that methionine (AUG) and tryptophan (UGG) have one codon each, so at those two positions there is no silent option]

3. Neutral, the substitution changes the mRNA codon and the amino acid translated, however the resulting amino acid substitution produces no detectable change in the function of the protein. Two named routes: substitution of the original amino acid with an amino acid of similar physical and chemical properties, or substitution of an amino acid residue that is non-essential to that protein's structure and function.

4. Missense, a different amino acid is translated, so the amino acid sequence of the polypeptide is changed, resulting in a change in the specific 3-dimensional conformation of the protein, and hence the function of the protein is altered.

5. Nonsense, a codon for an amino acid is changed into a stop codon, leading to the premature termination of translation. The resulting polypeptide is shorter (truncated) than normal, and nearly all nonsense mutations result in non-functional proteins.

6. So three of the four possible outcomes of a substitution leave a working protein and only one of them reliably does not. That is the whole basis of the prediction.

The insertion, max 6:

7. One base is not a multiple of three, and the resulting mRNA is read as a series of non-overlapping codons, so an insertion not in multiples of three results in a frameshift mutation. The code is triplet and non-overlapping and the reading frame is set by the start codon AUG. [CROSS-CLUSTER: Cluster 2]

8. All the nucleotides downstream of the insertion site are improperly grouped into codons, resulting in extensive missense, the amino acid sequence from that point on is completely altered, not altered at one residue.

9. The frameshift may also cause a new, premature stop codon to be generated in the reading frame, or a read-through of the normal stop codon, resulting in polypeptides of altered lengths. In any case, a frameshift usually results in a non-functional protein.

10. Nothing upstream of the site changes, so position decides how much is lost. The change sits at codon 12 of 400, so roughly 97% of the polypeptide lies downstream and is rewritten. The same insertion at codon 395 would cost far less.

11. The chain to loss of function has to be written out, and it is the same chain either way: primary structure changed → R groups in different positions → different hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, hydrophobic interactions and disulfide bonds → changed tertiary conformation → active site or binding site no longer complementary in shape to the substrate → non-functional protein. [CROSS-BOOK, Book 1]

12. Judgement, and it must be conditional rather than absolute: the substitution is more likely but not certain to leave function, because it can still be missense at a catalytic or binding residue, or nonsense; the insertion is very unlikely to leave function at this position.

R: calling a substitution a frameshift, no base has been added or removed, so the frame cannot shift. R: treating every insertion or deletion as catastrophic without applying the multiple-of- three test. R: "the gene is faulty so the protein doesn't work", which skips every marking point.

(b) A third patient carries that same insertion in the cells of a tumour, but not in his blood and not in his sperm. State what follows from this for him and for any children he has. [4]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) What follows from a mutation present in a tumour but not in blood or sperm. [4]

1. The change is present only in a somatic cell and its descendants, so it is a somatic mutation, not a germline one.

2. Somatic mutations occur in somatic cells and are not inherited by the progeny, so none of his children can inherit it and it is lost on the death of the organism.

3. It affects only the individual, and only the clone of cells descended from the mutated cell, which is what the tumour is.

4. Contrast, for the second mark: a germline mutation occurs in germline cells (germ cells and gametes) and may be transmitted to the offspring and to successive generations; when a mutated gamete fuses with another gamete the resulting zygote contains the mutation, and mitosis then transmits it to every cell of the new individual. If adverse, the mutant condition is a genetic disorder / hereditary disease.

Sources & concepts

Source: ACJC Prelim 2015 P2 Q10b [6] (a, the deletion-versus-multiple-of-three split and the chain from changed R groups through 3D configuration to a non-complementary active site, verbatim from the key, which runs it on DNA polymerase III); School Prelim 2023 P2 Q4b and HCI Prelim 2023 P2 Q4b, reprinted as Topical 2019 STQ Q4d(ii) from EJC Prelim 2020 P2 Q1(d)(ii) (a, the eight-point frameshift-to-non-functional-enzyme key and the shorter EJC version, verbatim); Topical 2019 STQ Q4d(i), from EJC Prelim 2020 P2 Q1(d)(i) [2] (a, missense against nonsense, verbatim, including "Reject references to degeneracy of genetic code" as a distinguishing feature); TPE 2024 P3 Q1a(ii) and TPE 2025 P3 Q1a(ii) [2] (a, why a substitution leaves the downstream amino acids alone, verbatim); SAJC Prelim 2021 P1 Q7, key B (a, the minimum-and-maximum reasoning that a base change need not change an amino acid); NJC Prelim 2020 P2 essay key and NYJC Prelim 2025 P3 Q4a (a, the multiples-of-three lists, verbatim). Part (b): CJC Prelim 2025 P3 Q1e [1] (verbatim, "It is a somatic mutation"); MI Prelim 2023 P2 Q4c [2] (verbatim, including zygote and mitosis); CJC Prelim 2017 P2 Q4bii [1]; DHS Prelim 2021 P1 Q20, key A. The tumour framing of (b) is [INFERRED: extension, no official key]. Archetype: mechanism explain-chain, run as a prediction between two named alternatives. Trap: the symmetrical pair. Claiming a single substitution shifts the reading frame, it cannot, because no base is added or removed. And treating every indel as catastrophic, when a 3-base deletion does not frameshift at all. Second trap: offering degeneracy as the difference between missense and nonsense, which is an explicit reject; degeneracy is why a silent mutation exists. LOs: 2(k) gene mutation, with substitution, addition and deletion including frameshift. Reach-back 2(c) translation and the genetic code, Core Idea 1 protein structure. Concepts fused: (1) substitution defined as replacement of one nucleotide pair; (2) the four substitution outcomes discriminated by two questions, did the amino acid change and did the function change; (3) degeneracy of the genetic code and where the redundancy sits; (4) the two amino acids with a single codon; (5) the two named routes to a neutral mutation; (6) premature stop codons and truncation; (7) the multiple-of-three test as the thing that decides everything about an indel; (8) triplet, non-overlapping code and the frame set by AUG; (9) extensive missense downstream against a single changed residue; (10) read-through of a normal stop codon as the other frameshift outcome; (11) position within the gene as a quantitative determinant of damage; (12) primary to tertiary to active site as the loss-of-function chain, reached back to Book 1; (13) germline against somatic and what each means for inheritance.

Question 2 [18 marks]

(a) Fig. 2.1 shows a red blood cell from an unaffected person and a red blood cell from a person with sickle cell anaemia.

Account for the difference between the two cells, and state what has not changed about the haemoglobin molecule. [12]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Account for the difference between the two cells in Fig. 2.1, and what has not changed. [12]

The chain, in order, max 9:

1. The gene involved is the β-globin gene, which encodes one of the polypeptide subunits that make up haemoglobin (Hb). The answer must start here, a scheme in this Book states "Reject marking points 1 and 2 if the answer just states 'at the 12th amino acid position' without the idea that it occurred in the DNA / gene."

2. There is a substitution of a thymine for an adenine at one position in the Hb gene (template strand), which results in a missense mutation. Quote one of the strings exactly: DNA triplet CTT → CAT, or mRNA codon GAG → GUG.

3. The sixth amino acid residue in the polypeptide is changed from a glutamate (hydrophilic) to a valine (hydrophobic). Both halves of that are needed; glutamate to valine on its own is half a point.

4. The specific three-dimensional conformation and function of the Hb protein is altered, because the primary structure changed, so the R groups form different interactions, where glutamate's charged R group made ionic bonds and hydrogen bonds, valine's non-polar R group makes hydrophobic interactions. [CROSS-BOOK, Book 1]

5. The substitution creates a hydrophobic spot on the outside of the Hb protein that sticks to the hydrophobic region of an adjacent Hb protein's beta chain.

6. The mutant Hb subunits stick to one another when the oxygen concentration is low, particularly when the red blood cells are in capillaries and veins, so HbS is less soluble at low oxygen concentrations and the molecules polymerise / crystallise. The aggregated proteins form fibre-like structures within red blood cells. It is reversible, at high oxygen concentration the haemoglobin resumes globular structure.

7. The fibre-like structures cause the red blood cells to lose their normal morphology and become sickle-shaped, which is the difference visible in Fig. 2.1: the unaffected cell is a smooth biconcave disc, the affected one a rigid crescent with pointed ends.

8. Two separate physiological consequences, both wanted: sickled cells are less able to move through capillaries and can block blood flow, resulting in severe pain and cell death of the surrounding tissue due to shortage in oxygen; and the sickled red blood cells are also fragile and easily destroyed, further decreasing the oxygen carrying capacity of blood.

9. The mutation is inherited, so it is germline and present in every cell from the zygote onwards, it is not something the red cell acquired. Note that one prelim stem in the corpus opens "Sickle cell anaemia is caused by a somatic mutation"; that premise is wrong.

What has not changed, max 3:

10. The number and type of subunits is unchanged. Haemoglobin is still the Book 1 worked example of quaternary structure: four polypeptide subunits, two α and two β, each associated with a haem prosthetic group holding an Fe²⁺ ion. [CROSS-BOOK, Book 1]

11. The molecular size is unchanged, HbA and HbS have the same molecular mass, and only one amino acid in one of the four subunits differs, so the primary structure is 99.8% the same.

12. What changed is the surface chemistry of the β subunit, which is exactly why HbS molecules stick to each other rather than falling apart. A whole-molecule change would destroy haemoglobin; a surface change makes it aggregate.

R: "the gene is faulty so the haemoglobin doesn't work." R: starting the chain at the amino acid. R: saying valine, or the red blood cell, or the polypeptide chain, polymerises, it is the HbS molecules that polymerise.

(b) The allele responsible is common in regions where malaria is endemic. Account for that, and decide whether the mutation is better called harmful or advantageous. [6]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Why the allele is common where malaria is endemic, and whether it is harmful or advantageous. [6]

1. In malarial regions HbAHbS heterozygotes have a higher reproductive success than either homozygote, so the allele is selected for and persists at high frequency despite being lethal in the homozygote.

2. HbSHbS homozygotes die of sickle cell anaemia, because sickle-shaped red blood cells obstruct blood vessels and deprive multiple organs of oxygen, resulting in organ damage, and because they are more rigid and fragile, haemolysing readily.

3. HbAHbA homozygotes die of malaria, because the malarial parasite (Plasmodium) can only infect normal red blood cells and not sickle-shaped ones.

4. The heterozygote makes both haemoglobins, so it has enough normal HbA for adequate oxygen transport and enough HbS for the parasite to be at a disadvantage, and it therefore survives and reproduces where both homozygotes do not.

5. The judgement has to name the level. At the level of the individual homozygote the mutation is harmful, it produces a painful, life-shortening disease. At the level of the population under a malarial selection pressure it is advantageous, because it raises mean fitness and changes allele frequency over time.

6. So "harmful or advantageous" is not answerable without saying which level and which selection pressure. Remove malaria from the environment and the same allele is purely deleterious, which is why its frequency tracks the distribution of malaria and not the distribution of people.

Sources & concepts

Source: DHS Prelim 2023 P3 Q4b [10] (a and b, the whole chain plus the heterozygote-advantage section, verbatim from the key, including "HbAHbA homozygotes die of malaria" and the reason); SAJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q4a [5] (a, the solubility version, verbatim, including "the R groups of valine form different interactions with other amino acids"); MI Prelim 2023 P2 Q4a [4] (a, verbatim, including the hydrophobic patch on the outside of the protein); NYJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q2a [2] (a, verbatim, with the reject on valine or the red blood cell polymerising); TMJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q6a [3] (a, verbatim, the hydrophobic R group of valine inserting into the hydrophobic pocket of another β-globin); JJC Prelim 2018 P3 Q1e(i) [4] and JJC Prelim 2017 P2 Q4a [1] (a, the five-step chain to capillary blockage and haemolysis, verbatim); DHS Prelim 2017 P2 Q5ci [1] (a, the mutation named as missense); MI Prelim 2023 P2 Q4c [2] (a, the germline point, and the source of the erroneous stem); NYJC Prelim 2025 P3 Q4a essay key (a and b). The figure is the school's own micrograph pair, 2.5 p. 14. The "what has not changed" half of (a) is [INFERRED: extension, no official key], built from Book 1's haemoglobin treatment. Archetype: mechanism explain-chain on the one disease the syllabus names, closed with a cross-book negative. Trap: starting the chain at the protein. The KRAS scheme in this Book rejects the first two marking points outright if the answer never mentions the DNA or the gene, and the same discipline applies here. Second trap: over-claiming that the whole haemoglobin molecule is wrecked, when the quaternary assembly is intact and only one surface residue in one subunit differs. LOs: 2(l) how gene mutations result in disease, including sickle cell anaemia. Also 2(k) substitution and missense. Reach-back Core Idea 1 protein structure and bonding. Concepts fused: (1) the named gene and the subunit it encodes; (2) the exact base change, quoted as a string; (3) missense classified, not just described; (4) hydrophilic glutamate to hydrophobic valine as a change in R-group chemistry; (5) which bonds are lost and which are gained, reached back to Book 1; (6) the exposed hydrophobic patch as a surface property; (7) oxygen concentration as the trigger, and reversibility; (8) polymerisation into fibres inside the cell; (9) two distinct physiological consequences, blockage and haemolysis; (10) germline inheritance as the reason every cell carries it; (11) haemoglobin's quaternary structure as the thing that did not change; (12) equal molecular size, which becomes the load-bearing fact in Q4(b); (13) heterozygote advantage as a population-level argument; (14) naming the level at which a judgement is being made.

Question 3 [16 marks]

(a) Apart from a polymerase, PCR uses none of the proteins that a cell uses to replicate its DNA. Account for how each of those jobs gets done instead, and identify the one requirement of the cellular process that PCR still cannot escape. [10]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) How PCR replaces the cell's replication proteins, and what it cannot escape. [10]

What replaces what, max 6:

1. Heat replaces helicase and the initiator proteins. The amplification is carried out in vitro, i.e. heat is used to separate the 2 DNA strands: at 90-100 °C (95 °C for about 30 s) the hydrogen bonds holding together the two strands of the DNA template are broken, so the template is denatured to single-stranded DNA. In the cell that work is done by helicase using ATP, and the origin is opened by initiator proteins. [CROSS-CLUSTER: Cluster 1]

2. The annealing temperature replaces the single-strand DNA-binding proteins. Cooling to 50-65 °C is enough to let primers anneal specifically to complementary sequences at the 3' end of the single-stranded templates via hydrogen bonds, but the temperature is kept high enough that the two long template strands do not re-anneal to each other. In the cell, re-annealing is prevented by single-strand binding proteins, which also protect the unstable ssDNA.

3. Chemically synthesised DNA primers replace primase. PCR uses two sets of short, single-stranded DNA primers, oligonucleotides about 20 bases long, made artificially, whereas the cell uses RNA primers made by primase. The distinction is a real examiner's point: RNA primers are only found in DNA replication; as synthetic primers are used during PCR there is no need to use RNA primers, which would then have to be replaced with DNA.

4. Nothing replaces DNA polymerase I or ligase, because neither is needed. In the cell, DNA polymerase I removes the RNA primer with 5'→3' exonuclease activity and replaces the ribonucleotides with DNA nucleotides, and ligase seals the phosphodiester bond between Okazaki fragments. In PCR the primers are DNA already and are kept in the product, and each new strand is synthesised continuously in one piece from a single primer, so there are no Okazaki fragments and no nicks to seal.

5. Nothing replaces topoisomerase, because the problem does not arise. In the cell, supercoiling builds ahead of a moving fork in a long, anchored, circular or packed molecule; in a tube the template is short, linear and already fully separated before synthesis begins, so there is no fork travelling into unopened duplex and no torque to relieve.

6. Taq polymerase replaces the cell's DNA polymerase III, and the buffer supplies Mg²⁺ ions as the cofactor required for DNA polymerase activity. Taq is thermostable and is not denatured by repeated heat treatments in the PCR cycle, so it need not be replaced each cycle.

What cannot be escaped, max 4:

7. DNA synthesis cannot occur de novo. None of the DNA polymerases can initiate the synthesis of a DNA strand on its own, because the shape of the active site is complementary to the 5' phosphate of the incoming nucleotide and the 3'-OH group of the last nucleotide of the growing strand. [CROSS-BOOK, Book 1, active-site complementarity]

8. So a primer is still required, purely to provide a free 3'-OH end that the polymerase can extend. That requirement is the one thing PCR keeps: it changes what the primer is made of and who makes it, but it cannot do without one.

9. The other two constraints survive as well. Elongation is still 5' to 3' only, with the template read 3' to 5', and the primer sequences flank the sequence of interest and are complementary to the 3' end of both template strands, which is why two primers are needed and why they set the boundaries of the product.

10. Synthesis is still by complementary base pairing, with phosphodiester bonds catalysed between the free 3'-OH of the growing strand and the 5' phosphate of the incoming dNTP, the incoming dNTP losing a pyrophosphate group whose bond breakage supplies the energy.

R: describing transformation of a host cell, or any step involving a plasmid, PCR is cell-free. R: "RNA primers" in a PCR answer.

(b) PCR is run on mitochondrial DNA extracted from a 30 000-year-old Neanderthal bone. Rank the limitations of PCR by how badly each threatens this particular experiment, and state which property of PCR makes the experiment possible at all. [6]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Ranking the limitations of PCR against a 30 000-year-old bone. [6]

1. The property that makes the experiment possible at all is sensitivity together with robustness: PCR can amplify sequences from trace amounts of DNA, down to a single cell, and permits amplification of specific sequences from material in which the DNA is badly degraded or embedded in a medium from which conventional DNA isolation is difficult. A few hours of cycling turns an unusable sample into enough DNA to sequence, because the number of copies doubles every cycle, giving 2ⁿ copies after n cycles.

2. First and worst, contamination. Due to the extreme sensitivity of PCR, any contamination of the reaction by non-template nucleic acids in the environment could be easily amplified. Here the contaminant is modern human DNA, from the excavator, the museum, the laboratory, which is very similar in sequence to the target, so it anneals to the same primers and the result may be an amplified modern human sequence reported as Neanderthal. This is the single fact that is advantage 1 and limitation 1 at the same time.

3. Second, infidelity. Taq polymerase lacks 3' to 5' exonuclease activity, so there is no proofreading, and the error rate is about 1 in 10 000 bases. It matters more than usual here because an error made in an early cycle is copied into every descendant molecule, and because the whole point of the experiment is to find the small number of positions at which Neanderthal differs from modern human, a genuine variant and a polymerase error look identical in the product. [CROSS-CLUSTER: Cluster 1: DNA polymerase III proofreads, reversing by one base pair and excising the mismatch, which is exactly the activity Taq is missing]

4. Third, prior sequence information is required to design the primers, and the only sequence available is the modern human one. If the Neanderthal sequence differs within a primer binding site, the primers are no longer complementary, cannot anneal, and nothing is amplified, a false negative rather than a wrong answer. A difference between the two primer sites would still be amplified.

5. Fourth and least threatening, the limited product size. PCR is efficient only over roughly 0.1-5 kb, but ancient DNA is already fragmented into short pieces, so short amplicons are what the experiment wants anyway. The limitation and the sample happen to agree.

6. Irrelevant here: PCR applies only to nucleic acids and not to proteins. True, and it costs this experiment nothing, since the target is mitochondrial DNA. Say so rather than listing it as a threat, the ranking is the mark.

Also creditable: Taq is stable at high temperatures and not denatured by repeated heat treatments, with a half-life of about 40 minutes at 95 °C against a denaturation step lasting about one minute, so many cycles fit inside one half-life. [CROSS-BOOK, Book 1: thermostability is a property of the bonds maintaining the tertiary structure, and 72 °C is Taq's optimum temperature, not merely a temperature it tolerates]

Sources & concepts

Source: 9477 Specimen P3 Q1(c)(i) [3] (b, the degraded-fossil-DNA framing is the official specimen's own, applied there to Neanderthal mtDNA); ASRJC Prelim 2021 P2 Q9a [1] (b, the Neanderthal fossil stem, verbatim); DHS Prelim 2023 P2 Q4b [2] (a, the six-row PCR-against-replication table, verbatim from the key); TJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q6c [2] (a, the similarity and difference lists against a replication fork diagram, verbatim, including the 55 °C re-annealing point); School Prelim 2024 P1 Q14 and HCI Prelim 2024 P1 Q14 (a, DNA primers not RNA primers, key C, 54.60% correct, with the examiner's comment reproduced in full); ASRJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q7a [2] and TJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q5c (a, the free 3'-OH and the active-site-complementarity argument, verbatim); JPJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q6a(i), (ii) and (iii) and SAJC Prelim 2024 P2 Q3(a) (a, the three steps with their reasons, verbatim); MI Prelim 2023 P2 Q5b(i)-(iii) [6] and ASRJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q4a [4] (a, the temperatures, verbatim); NYJC Prelim 2025 P3 Q1e(i) [4] (a, Taq's role, verbatim); CJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q5d [2] (b, the advantage and limitation lists, verbatim); JPJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q6c [1] (b, the four limitations, verbatim); YIJC Prelim 2023 P3 Q2a(ii) [2] (b, thermostability against the loss of proofreading, verbatim); TMJC Prelim 2023 P1 Q18, key D (b, the advantage-and-limitation grid); VJC Prelim 2025 P1 Q16, key D (b, a mutation inside the primer binding site prevents amplification); MI Prelim 2023 P2 Q5d [2] (the half-life reasoning, verbatim). The ranking in (b) is the extension. Archetype: technique procedure plus purpose, the dominant archetype in this chapter at 51% of its corpus, inverted so that the purpose is argued rather than recited. Trap: describing PCR as if it happened in a cell, transformation, plasmids, a host organism. PCR is in vitro and cell-free. Second trap: naming a step without its purpose, which the schemes here reject consistently. Third trap: forgetting that the advantages and limitations are written into LO 2(j)(i) and are a separate node from the procedure, the corpus files 54 questions on the procedure and only 13 on what PCR can and cannot do. LOs: 2(j)(i) the principles and procedures of PCR, including its advantages and limitations. Reach-back 2(b) DNA replication and its enzymes, Core Idea 1 enzymes. Concepts fused: (1) denaturation by heat as the functional replacement for helicase; (2) the annealing temperature doing the job of single-strand binding proteins; (3) synthetic DNA primers against primase-made RNA primers; (4) why DNA polymerase I and ligase have no counterpart in a tube; (5) why supercoiling never arises, argued from the geometry of the template; (6) Taq, its optimum and its thermostability; (7) Mg²⁺ as the cofactor; (8) the de-novo prohibition and the active-site geometry behind it; (9) the free 3'-OH as the one requirement that survives; (10) directionality and the two-primer requirement as boundary-setting; (11) exponential amplification as 2ⁿ; (12) sensitivity as advantage and limitation in one fact; (13) absence of proofreading and error propagation through cycles; (14) primer design as a dependency on prior sequence knowledge, and what a mutated primer site does; (15) ranking constraints against a specific experiment rather than reciting them.

Question 4 [16 marks]

(a) Fig. 4.1 shows the products of a PCR run on DNA from three deer mice, using primers that flank a gene whose mutant allele carries a deletion.

Account for every feature of the pattern in Fig. 4.1, and state what this gel cannot establish. [10]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Account for the pattern in Fig. 4.1, and state what the gel cannot establish. [10]

Why the DNA moves, and why it separates, max 4:

1. The phosphate groups of the sugar-phosphate backbone in DNA are negatively-charged, so DNA moves towards the positive electrode (anode) once a direct current is applied. The arrow in Fig. 4.1 points down the gel, so the wells are at the top, at the negatively-charged cathode, and the anode is at the bottom. [CROSS-CLUSTER: Cluster 1: the phosphates project outward from the helix because they are hydrophilic, which is why the whole molecule carries a uniform surface charge]

2. DNA molecules essentially have a constant charge density, i.e. charge per unit of mass, so charge cancels out of the comparison between fragments and they separate primarily on the basis of size. This is the whole answer to "why size and not charge", and an answer without it is incomplete.

3. The complex network of pores in the gel matrix acts as a molecular sieve that impedes movement and separates the fragments by length. Shorter DNA fragments are less impeded by the pores than longer ones and move through the gel more quickly, so fragments of different lengths migrate as distinct bands.

4. The PCR products are linear, which they must be, "DNA molecules to be separated by electrophoresis should be linear", and agarose is the appropriate gel for products of this size, separating over roughly 0.5-20 kb.

Reading the three lanes, max 4:

5. The mutant allele carries a deletion, so the amplified product of the normal allele is longer than the amplified product of the mutant allele. The upper band is therefore the normal allele and the lower band the mutant allele, because DNA fragments from the normal gene travel a shorter distance.

6. Deer mouse 1 shows the upper band only, so it carries two copies of the normal allele and is homozygous normal.

7. Deer mouse 2 shows the lower band only, so it carries two copies of the mutated allele and is homozygous mutant. Deer mouse 3 shows both bands, so it carries one copy of each and is heterozygous.

8. Consequence, if asked to go on: deer mouse 2 and deer mouse 3 will probably die of a severe viral infection, because they have two copies and one copy of the mutated allele respectively, so insufficient antiviral proteins are produced.

What the gel cannot establish, max 3:

9. No sizes. There is no molecular weight marker / DNA ladder lane on this gel. A ladder contains DNA fragments of known length and allows the size determination of the bands; without one, the gel gives relative positions only, so nothing can be said about how many base pairs either allele is, or how large the deletion is. Gels run under different conditions are also not directly comparable.

10. No sequence, and therefore no substitutions. A gel reports the sizes present and the number of distinct fragments, and nothing about base order. A mutation that does not change the length of the amplified product, a substitution, or a single-base indel inside a long product, leaves the band in the same place and would be invisible: the two products would not appear as separate bands and would travel the same distance. Nor can the gel say which allele is dominant, whether either mouse is actually ill, or whether the deletion is inside a coding region.

R: reversing the migration, DNA runs towards the anode and small fragments end up furthest from the well. R: calling fragment size "inversely proportional" to distance migrated; the relationship is logarithmic.

(b) Haemoglobin extracted from an unaffected person, from a carrier and from a person with sickle cell anaemia is separated on a gel at alkaline pH. Predict the three lanes and account for the separation. [6]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Predict and account for the three haemoglobin lanes at alkaline pH. [6]

1. At alkaline pH, HbA and HbS are negatively charged and migrate towards the positive electrode, so this separation, like the DNA one, is driven by an applied field acting on a net negative charge.

2. There the resemblance stops. Glutamate has a charged, hydrophilic R group and valine a non-polar one, so replacing glutamate with valine at position 6 removes one negatively charged amino acid from each β chain, and haemoglobin has two β chains per molecule. [CROSS-BOOK, Book 1 R-group chemistry and quaternary structure]

3. Therefore one less negatively charged amino acid (glutamic acid) in HbS results in slower migration across the gel, HbS is less strongly attracted to the anode and travels a shorter distance from the well in the same time.

4. Reject size. HbA and HbS are of the same molecular size, so the sieving argument that carried the whole of part (a) earns nothing here. Proteins of the same mass separate by charge; DNA fragments of different length separate by size, precisely because their charge per unit mass is constant. Importing one explanation into the other is the mark this question exists to take.

5. The three lanes: the unaffected person gives a single band at the HbA position, furthest migrated; the person with sickle cell anaemia gives a single band at the HbS position, less far migrated; the carrier gives two bands, one at each position.

6. Thickness is a mark of its own. The carrier's two bands are each about half the thickness of the homozygotes' single bands, because the carrier makes roughly half as much of each haemoglobin. Reference lanes of known HbA and HbS are run alongside so that band positions can be matched to a known genotype.

Sources & concepts

Source: NYJC Prelim 2025 P3 Q1e(ii) [2] and Q1e(iii) [4] (a, the deer mouse stem, Fig. 1.4 and both keys, verbatim, including "Deer mouse 2 and 3" and the four-point electrophoresis explanation); TMJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q6b(iii) [3] (a, the negatively charged phosphates, the anode and the molecular sieve, verbatim); NJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q6c [3] (a, the four principles, verbatim); CJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q5ai [1] (a, the electrode labelling and its reason, verbatim, and the DNA ladder's definition); School Prelim 2023 P2 Q4d and HCI Prelim 2023 P2 Q4d [3] (a, "No, it cannot detect base substitutions… no change in length… would not appear as separate bands", verbatim with its accept and reject list); YIJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q5a(iii) [1] (a, agarose resolution and the examiner's comment about what the presence of a ladder rules out); SAJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q5e [2] (a, the reject on a substitution changing band position); RVHS Prelim 2023 P2 Q6b [4] (a, shorter fragment migrates furthest, verbatim). Part (b): SAJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q4b [1] (verbatim, including "[Reject: size, as HbA and HbS are of the same molecular size]"); NYJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q2c(i) and SAJC Prelim 2024 P2 Q3(b)(i) [4] (verbatim, the six-point any-four list); NYJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q2c(ii) and SAJC Prelim 2024 P2 Q3(b)(ii) [2] (the banding prediction and the thickness rule, verbatim); TMJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q6c(i) [1] (the purpose of the known-genotype reference lanes, verbatim, with "control" rejected). The figure is NYJC's own Fig. 1.4. Archetype: data / figure interpretation, the largest archetype in the Book, closed with a discrimination between two separation mechanisms. Trap: the migration reversal, DNA is negative, so it runs towards the anode, and small fragments end up furthest from the well. Reversing either half loses a mark you understood. Second trap, and the one part (b) is built on: reading a protein gel as a size separation. The scheme rejects it outright, because HbA and HbS are the same molecular size. Third trap: concluding sizes from a gel with no ladder. LOs: 2(j)(ii) the principles and procedures of gel electrophoresis. Also 2(l) sickle cell at the protein level and 2(k) deletion. Reach-back 2(a) the sugar-phosphate backbone, Core Idea 1 amino acid R groups and quaternary structure. Concepts fused: (1) negatively charged phosphates and the direction of migration; (2) constant charge density as the reason charge drops out of the comparison; (3) the gel as a molecular sieve; (4) the linear-DNA requirement and the working range of agarose; (5) mapping band position to allele length when the mutant carries a deletion; (6) homozygote against heterozygote read off a lane; (7) the DNA ladder and what its absence forfeits; (8) what a gel cannot report, sequence, and therefore substitutions; (9) protein separation by charge at alkaline pH; (10) the charge consequence of glutamate to valine, which is the same substitution as Q2 used for a different property; (11) two β chains per molecule, so two charges lost per haemoglobin; (12) equal molecular size as an explicit reject; (13) band thickness as a quantitative signal of gene dosage; (14) reference lanes of known genotype.

Question 5 [16 marks]

(a) Fig. 5.1 shows a stained agarose gel of digested genomic DNA beside the autoradiogram of a Southern blot made from the same lane of that gel.

Account for the difference between the two images, and give the procedure that turns one into the other. [10]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) The difference between the gel and the autoradiogram, and the procedure between them. [10]

Why the two images differ, max 3:

1. Lane 2 is whole genomic DNA cut into fragments, which produces hundreds of thousands of fragments of every possible length. They overlap continuously all the way down the lane, so they cannot resolve into discrete bands and appear as a smear. Lane 1 resolves cleanly only because it is one small DNA cut into a handful of fragments of known length, 23.1 kb down to 2.0 kb.

2. The autoradiogram shows a small number of discrete dark bands because only those fragments that contain a sequence complementary to the probe hybridise with it, so only those carry a label and only those are visualised.

3. Every other fragment is still on the membrane, it has simply not been labelled. This is the entire point of the technique: it turns "here are all the fragments" into "here is the one I care about", which is why a smear on the gel can still yield a readable result.

The procedure, one mark per step with its purpose, max 7:

4. Cut. The DNA is digested into fragments by restriction enzymes, which is what makes a length difference between alleles visible at all. (Naming this step is required; nothing about the enzymes themselves is.)

5. Separate. The fragments are separated on the basis of size by agarose gel electrophoresis, with molecular weight markers electrophoresed alongside in lane 1.

6. Denature. The double-stranded DNA molecules must be denatured to their single-stranded form before hybridisation with the probe, and this is done either prior to or during the blotting process by exposing the gel to alkaline denaturing conditions / NaOH. Without this there is nothing for a single-stranded probe to base-pair with. [CROSS-CLUSTER: Cluster 1: what is being broken is the hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs]

7. Transfer. The gel is supported on a wick or sponge in a bath of buffer, a nitrocellulose or nylon membrane is laid over it, and a stack of blotting paper is placed on top; capillary action draws the buffer up through the gel and the membrane, carrying the DNA with it and transferring it as a replica of the band positions on the gel. The membrane is then baked at about 80 °C, or exposed to UV, to fix the DNA permanently onto it.

8. Hybridise. The membrane is sealed in a bag with a buffered salt solution containing a labelled single-stranded DNA or RNA probe, which hybridises with the DNA of interest by complementary base pairing. The probe is labelled, i.e. carries a radioactive, fluorescent or chemical marker to facilitate detection, and is complementary in nucleotide sequence to the specific target sequence it binds.

9. Wash and detect. The membrane is washed to remove unbound probe, then subjected to autoradiography, an X-ray film is placed over the membrane, so that dark bands appear exactly where the probe has base-paired.

10. Read. The size of the DNA that hybridises with the probe can be determined by reference to the molecular weight markers that were electrophoresed alongside, which is why lane 1 is in the picture at all.

R: reciting the steps without their purposes. R: giving a probe that is double-stranded, or unlabelled, or complementary to only one of the two alleles when both need detecting.

(b) Fig. 5.2 shows one labelled probe and one mixture of single-stranded DNA molecules, incubated at two different temperatures.

Account for the difference between the two outcomes, then decide which condition you would use to search another species for a related gene, and whether the same molecule could serve as a PCR primer. [6]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) The two temperatures in Fig. 5.2, the choice for a related gene, and probe against primer. [6]

1. Hybridisation is the process by which two complementary, single-stranded nucleic acid chains base-pair and reform a double-stranded hybrid. Crucially, nucleic acid sequences do not need to be perfectly complementary to be able to hybridise, and the stringency of hybridisation can be controlled by varying the incubation temperature.

2. At 42 °C the conditions are more stringent. The temperature sits just below the melting point of a perfectly base-paired helix, so all imperfect helices are unstable and dissociate. Only A, the identical match, forms a stable double helix.

3. At 35 °C the conditions are less stringent. Imperfectly paired double helices can form and remain stable, so A, C and E all form stable double helices, Fig. 5.2 marks the bulges as imperfect base-pairing. C and E are related but non-identical sequences.

4. So the choice of temperature is a choice of question. To search another species for a related gene, use the lower, less stringent temperature, because a homologous gene in a different species will be similar but not identical and would be missed at high stringency. The cost is specificity: sequences that merely resemble the target are also picked up, so the result needs confirming. [CROSS-CLUSTER: Cluster 1: a G-C pair is held by 3 hydrogen bonds and an A-T pair by 2, so a GC-rich duplex melts at a higher temperature, which is also why a primer low in GC content needs a lower annealing temperature]

5. Probe against primer. Both are single-stranded oligonucleotides which bind to the DNA via complementary base-pairing. The difference is what they are for: a primer anneals to a specific sequence on the DNA template and provides a free 3'-OH group for DNA polymerase to add nucleotides to, whereas a probe allows the detection of target DNA in a sample and is therefore structurally modified, i.e. labelled, to carry a radioactive, fluorescent or chemical marker.

6. So the judgement is no, not reliably. A probe ranges from 15 to several thousand nucleotides long, where a primer is about 20 bases; PCR needs two primers flanking the target, not one; and the mismatched binding that Fig. 5.2 shows a probe tolerating at 35 °C would destroy the specificity PCR depends on, the whole point of a primer is that it does not attach elsewhere.

Sources & concepts

Source: YIJC Prelim 2023 P3 Q2b(ii) [4] (a, the alkaline denaturation, nitrocellulose transfer, radioactive probe, wash and autoradiography chain, verbatim from the key, set on exactly this situation of a genomic digest giving smears instead of bands); YIJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q5b [6] (a, the six-step blotting procedure including the sponge, the paper towels, capillary action and the 80 °C bake, verbatim); MI Prelim 2023 P2 Q6d [4] (a, the four-step outline, verbatim); YIJC Prelim 2023 P1 Q14, key A (a, why whole-genome extraction forces a Southern blot where a PCR product would not); SAJC Prelim 2023 P1 Q21, key A (a, the purpose of the transfer step itself); RI Prelim 2024 P3 Q5(a) [15] marking points 16-20 (a, verbatim, including "transferred to a nitrocellulose membrane" and the autoradiography line); ASRJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q7c(i) [2] (b, the probe is single-stranded and complementary to the specific allele it binds, verbatim); NJC Prelim 2023 P1 Q19, key B (b, the primer-against-probe row: both are short single-stranded DNA, probes are labelled and primers are not); RI Prelim 2024 P1 Q22, key A (b, lower GC content requires a lower annealing temperature); CJC Prelim 2025 P3 Q2a [2] (b, why primer length is constrained at both ends). Both figures are the school's own, 2.6 pp. 15 and 17. The choice-of-stringency judgement and the probe-as-primer question are extensions. Archetype: technique procedure plus purpose, closed with a design decision. Trap: losing the denaturation step, or putting it in the wrong place. A double-stranded fragment cannot hybridise with a single-stranded probe, and the schemes place the alkaline denaturation before or during blotting, not after. Second trap: assuming a probe must match perfectly, the whole of part (b) turns on the fact that it need not. Third trap: describing a Southern blot as a way of separating DNA; separation has already happened on the gel, and the blot only identifies. LOs: 2(j)(iii) Southern blotting and nucleic acid hybridisation, and 2(j)(ii) as the first step. Reach-back 2(a) complementary base pairing and hydrogen bonding. Concepts fused: (1) why a genomic digest smears and a marker lane does not; (2) probe specificity as the reason the blot shows fewer bands than the gel; (3) the fate of the unlabelled fragments; (4) restriction digestion named as step one without any enzyme content; (5) size separation as step two; (6) alkaline denaturation and why it must precede hybridisation; (7) capillary transfer and fixing; (8) the labelled single-stranded probe and what "labelled" means; (9) washing and autoradiography; (10) reading sizes against the marker lane; (11) hybridisation defined; (12) stringency as a controllable variable; (13) what high and low stringency each select for; (14) choosing stringency to fit a biological question, and paying for it in specificity; (15) melting temperature and GC content as the underlying chemistry; (16) primer against probe, point for point.

Question 6 [18 marks]

(a) A single unequal crossing over between synapsed chromosomes at meiosis produces two abnormal chromosomes at once. Identify both, and account for the fact that one of them is usually far more damaging than the other. [8]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) The two products of one unequal crossing over, and why one is worse. [8]

1. A single unequal crossing over between synapsed chromosomes during meiosis produces, in the same event, a duplication on one chromatid and a deletion on the other, one chromatid gains a segment and its partner loses the same segment.

Deletion, max 4:

2. Deletion, a chromosome breaks in one or more places and a portion of it is lost. The loss can occur near one end or from the interior, giving a terminal or an intercalary deletion.

3. The effects are usually profound, because the genotype is altered due to the absence of certain gene loci, the information is simply gone and no copy remains on that chromosome.

4. If the deletion affects the same gene loci on both homologous chromosomes, the effect is usually lethal, since no functional copy of those loci exists anywhere in the cell.

5. If only one of a homologous pair is affected, the effect on the phenotype is that alleles on the non-deficient homologue will be expressed, even if recessive. This is the discriminating mark and almost nobody writes it: a deletion can unmask a recessive allele that would otherwise have been hidden, so a heterozygous carrier can become an affected individual without any new gene mutation at all.

Duplication, max 3:

6. Duplication, any part of the genetic material, be it a single locus or a large piece of chromosome, is present more than once in the genome. It can also arise from a replication error prior to meiosis.

7. Nothing has been lost, so the immediate consequences are milder: the effects are gene redundancy and phenotypic variation, and duplication is an important source of genetic variation during evolution, because a spare copy is free to accumulate mutations while the original continues to do its job.

8. Judgement: losing information is worse than holding it twice. A missing locus cannot be compensated for, and it additionally exposes whatever allele survives on the homologue, whereas an extra copy usually costs only altered gene dosage. The asymmetry is why one event that produces both is remembered for the deletion.

(b) Fig. 6.1 shows a reciprocal translocation in which no genetic material is lost and none is gained.

Account for the fact that a carrier of the rearrangement in Fig. 6.1 can still be affected, can have affected children, and can transmit Down syndrome to a child whose karyotype shows 46 chromosomes. Then decide whether an inversion of a segment of the same length would carry the same risks. [10]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Why a balanced translocation still causes harm, the 46-chromosome Down syndrome, and the inversion comparison. [10]

1. A reciprocal translocation involves the exchange of segments between two non-homologous chromosomes. Non-homologous is the load-bearing word, exchange between homologues is crossing over, which is normal. Genetic information is not lost or gained, there is only a rearrangement of genetic material, and hence the presence of a translocation does not directly alter the viability of individuals bearing it.

Why a carrier can still be affected, max 3:

2. Position effect. A translocation may realign certain genes in relation to other genes, so a gene carried to a new neighbourhood is transcribed at a different rate. Cluster 2 supplies the mechanism: enhancers and silencers are DNA sequences that act over hundreds or thousands of base pairs, work independently of their orientation, and may lie inside an intron, and activators bind enhancers to raise the transcription rate while repressors bind silencers to lower it. Move a gene next to a different set of control elements and its expression changes even though its own sequence is untouched. [CROSS-CLUSTER: Cluster 2]

3. A break point inside a gene. The two breaks have to fall somewhere, and if one falls within a coding sequence it destroys that gene, or fuses it to part of another, producing a protein that does not exist in a normal cell.

4. So "no material lost or gained" describes the chromosome complement, not the phenotype. The inventory is balanced; the arrangement is not.

Why the children can be affected, max 3:

5. A rearranged chromosome cannot pair normally at meiosis with its unrearranged partner, so segregation is disorderly and some gametes receive a duplication of a segment while others receive a deletion of it, unbalanced gametes.

6. The unbalanced gamete carries a duplication or deletion of genetic material and may give rise to an abnormal embryo on fertilisation by a normal gamete. The parent is unaffected precisely because the parent's own complement is balanced.

7. Down syndrome without 47 chromosomes. In a Robertsonian translocation the long arms of two chromosomes fuse, most often chromosome 21 onto chromosome 14, and the two short arms are lost with no effect. Such a carrier has 45 chromosomes, a balanced complement and a normal phenotype. Their gamete carrying both the 14/21 fusion chromosome and a free chromosome 21 delivers three copies of the chromosome-21 loci while the count reads 46, so the karyotype looks normal and the gene dosage is not. Non-disjunction accounts for 95% of Down syndrome; the other 5% are caused by translocation, mosaicism or partial trisomy.

The inversion comparison, max 3:

8. Inversion, a segment of a chromosome is turned around 180° within a chromosome. It requires two breaks along the length of the chromosome and subsequent reinsertion of the inverted segment, and it does not involve a loss of genetic information but simply rearranges the linear sequence.

9. So it shares two of the three risks: it may cause position effects, for the same reason, genes have been moved relative to control elements, and it has two break points that can fall inside a gene. It also produces aberrant gametes in heterozygotes, because an inverted segment cannot pair with its uninverted partner without looping.

10. The difference is the third route. An inversion keeps every locus on its own chromosome, so it cannot deliver an extra copy of a whole chromosome arm to a gamete and cannot produce a trisomy-equivalent child. A carrier of an inversion risks unbalanced gametes; a carrier of a Robertsonian translocation risks a specific, named, recurrent aneuploidy.

Sources & concepts

Source: IJC Prelim 2018 P2 Q4ai [1] (a, the unequal crossing over figure and the naming of both products in one answer, verbatim); RVHS Prelim 2023 P2 Q6c [3] (a, reading a duplication in one lane and a deletion in another off a real gel, verbatim, with translocation rejected); NYJC Prelim 2025 P3 Q4a essay key [12] (a and b, the four structural aberrations defined, verbatim); ASRJC Prelim 2021 P3 Q1a [4] (a, the gene-mutation against chromosomal-aberration comparison, verbatim, including "reshuffling of existing alleles"); EJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q4ci and ACJC Prelim 2018 P2 Q6a [2] (a, verbatim). Part (b): School Prelim 2023 P1 Q17, key D, 80.86% correct (the unbalanced gamete giving an abnormal embryo, and the three rejects, a somatic stem cell does not undergo meiosis, translocation is not non-disjunction, and a translocation does not produce a trisomy by adding a whole chromosome); CJC Prelim 2023 P1 Q11, key C (what can cause a translocation, end-to-end fusion, meiosis and unequal crossing over); DHS Prelim 2023 P1 Q22 (the Robertsonian 14/21 fusion, verbatim stem); EJC Prelim 2021 P3 Q3a (the 45-chromosome carrier karyotype with a 14-21 fusion, verbatim); RI Prelim 2017 P1 Q5, reprinted as JJC Prelim 2017 P1 Q17 and IJC Prelim 2018 P1 Q16, key D (the sperm-and-embryo grid that fixes 2n = 46 with Down syndrome as the possible outcome and 2n = 47 as the impossible one); NJC Prelim 2023 P1 Q16 and SAJC Prelim 2023 P1 Q5 (the 13-21 carrier version); CJC Prelim 2014 P1 Q14, key D (inversion identified against translocation and deletion); CJC Prelim 2018 P3 Q3a [3] (how chromosome fusion occurs). The figure is the school's own Fig. 14, 2.5 p. 20. The 95/5 split is 2.5 p. 27. The inversion comparison is [INFERRED: extension, no official key], because inversion is untested anywhere in the 343-question corpus and appears only inside mark-scheme lists. Archetype: compare / distinguish closed with a prediction on an untested type. Trap: treating "no genetic material is lost or gained" as though it meant "no consequence". The scheme's own wording is that a translocation does not directly alter viability, and the word doing the work is directly. Second trap: calling a translocation a gene mutation, Specimen P2 Q3(d) sets exactly that discrimination and rewards translocation as a chromosomal aberration against substitution as a gene mutation. Third trap: saying a translocation causes trisomy by adding a whole chromosome, which the prelim key rejects outright. LOs: 2(k) chromosomal aberration, structural, including translocation, duplication, inversion and deletion. Reach-back 2(i)(ii) control elements and transcription factors, 2(h) non-coding DNA. Concepts fused: (1) one meiotic error producing two different aberrations; (2) deletion defined, with terminal and intercalary; (3) lethality when both homologues lose the same loci; (4) unmasking of a recessive allele on the surviving homologue; (5) duplication defined, and its two origins; (6) gene redundancy and duplication as raw material for evolution; (7) ranking two aberrations by whether the information still exists; (8) reciprocal translocation defined, with non-homologous as the discriminator against crossing over; (9) position effect, mechanised through Cluster 2's enhancers and silencers; (10) a break point falling inside a gene; (11) unbalanced gametes from abnormal pairing; (12) the Robertsonian route to trisomy-21 dosage at a normal chromosome count; (13) the 95/5 split; (14) inversion defined, with two breaks and 180°; (15) transferring a mechanism to an untested case and identifying the one risk that does not carry over.

Question 7 [16 marks]

(a) Fig. 7.1 shows non-disjunction happening at two different points in meiosis.

One child with Down syndrome has the genotype P1 P2 P3 for a gene on chromosome 21 that has four alleles in the population; the mother is P1 P2 and the father is P3 P4. Using Fig. 7.1, deduce in which parent and at which division the failure occurred. [10]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Deduce which parent and which division, using Fig. 7.1. [10]

The mechanism, max 5:

1. Non-disjunction is the failure of chromosomes or chromatids to disjoin and move to opposite poles during division. When it occurs in meiosis, the normal distribution of chromosomes into gametes is disrupted.

2. It happens because the kinetochore fails to capture, or fails to hold, the spindle microtubules. The centromere is the site at which the kinetochore assembles, and if spindle fibres cannot attach, the pair is not pulled apart. [CROSS-CLUSTER: Cluster 1: the centromere nucleates the kinetochore, which is the protein complex that attaches to the microtubules of the spindle, and without attachment no poleward force acts]

3. Fig. 7.1(a), meiosis I: the homologous chromosomes fail to separate. Both members of the pair travel to the same pole, so all four gametes are abnormal, n+1, n+1, n−1, n−1, and the n+1 gamete carries both homologues, therefore both of that parent's alleles at the locus.

4. Fig. 7.1(b), meiosis II: the sister chromatids fail to separate. Meiosis I has already separated the homologues correctly, so only one of the two secondary cells is affected and the gametes are n+1, n−1, n, n, two abnormal and two normal. The n+1 gamete carries two copies of one chromatid, therefore the same allele twice.

5. That contrast is the whole deduction: meiosis I gives you two different alleles from one parent, meiosis II gives you the same allele twice.

The deduction, max 5:

6. The child is P1 P2 P3. The mother is P1 P2 and the father is P3 P4, so P1 and P2 both came from the mother and P3 came from the father.

7. Since the child has P1 P2 P3, and his mother has P1 and P2, non-disjunction must have occurred in the mother, a normal ovum could only have carried one of her two alleles.

8. Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes, and would have separated P1 and P2 during normal formation of the ovum in the mother. Since the child has both P1 and P2, non-disjunction must have occurred during meiosis I, where the pair of homologous chromosome 21 fail to separate, pulling the pair of homologous chromosomes to one pole.

9. The alternative is excluded explicitly. If non-disjunction occurred during meiosis II, the ovum would contain either P1 P1 or P2 P2, and the child would have the genotype P1 P1 P3 or P2 P2 P3, not the genotype observed. The father contributed a normal n gamete carrying P3.

10. So: the mother, at meiosis I. That (n+1) ovum fused with a normal (n) sperm, giving a zygote of 2n + 1 = 47 chromosomes, with an additional chromosome for the 21st pair.

(b) A second child carries the extra chromosome 21 in some of his cells but not in others, and non-disjunction is again responsible. Deduce when and in what kind of division that must have happened, and name precisely what the consequence of non-disjunction should be called. [6]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) When and in what division the mosaic form arose, and the correct name for the consequence. [6]

1. In the mosaic form the aberration affects only a proportion of the cells of the individual, while the rest carry the usual two copies.

2. A meiotic error affects the gamete and therefore every cell of the individual, because the zygote itself would carry it and mitosis would transmit it to all cells. That is the classic form, and it cannot produce a mosaic.

3. Therefore the zygote must have started with the normal chromosome number and the error must have happened after fertilisation, during a mitotic division in the developing embryo or foetus.

4. Non-disjunction of chromosome 21 at that mitosis gives one daughter cell with three copies of chromosome 21 and one with a single copy; the trisomic cell divides on to give a clone of trisomic cells alongside the normal cells, which is exactly what mosaicism is. The earlier in development it happens, the larger the affected clone.

5. Naming. The consequence of non-disjunction is aneuploidy, the general condition in which an organism loses or gains one or more chromosomes, but not a complete set. Monosomy is the loss of a single chromosome from an otherwise diploid genome (2n−1) and trisomy is the gain of one chromosome (2n+1).

6. Two refusals, both taken from examiners' comments. "Polyploidy" is wrong, because non-disjunction leads to an unequal distribution of the chromosomes, not the creation of an entire set of chromosomes; polyploidy means multiples of the haploid chromosome set and occurs mainly in plants, not animals. "Down syndrome" is refused as the name of the general consequence, because the preamble does not give sufficient information that the outcome will definitely be Down syndrome, and aneuploidy is a more accurate representation.

Sources & concepts

Source: TMJC Prelim 2023 P1 Q13, key A (a, the P1 P2 P3 stem and the whole deduction, verbatim from the key, including the meiosis II counterfactual giving P1 P1 P3 or P2 P2 P3; opening the MCQ out into a structured question is the extension); ASRJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q4c [3] (a, the centromere to kinetochore to spindle to non-disjunction chain and the n+1 and n−1 gametes, verbatim, with polyploidy rejected); IJC Prelim 2018 P2 Q4b [4] (a, the four-point trisomy key, verbatim); School Prelim 2025 P1 Q16 and NJC Prelim 2024 P1 Q16, key A, 45.66% correct (a, which parental divisions can and cannot give an XXY child, with the reasoning about what meiosis II can produce reproduced in full); ASRJC Prelim 2022 P1 Q14 and NYJC Prelim 2023 P1 Q15, key A (a, aneuploidy against polyploidy, and how an n−1 gamete gives 2n−1). Part (b): 9477 Specimen P1 Q15, key B [OFFICIAL] (the classic-against- mosaic stem, set by Cambridge itself); MI Prelim 2021 P1 Q10, key A, and SAJC Prelim 2021 P1 Q6, key C (the same three-route stem, both keying mitotic non-disjunction in the embryo only); ACJC Prelim 2023 P1 Q16, key D (mosaic Klinefelter by the same route); YIJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q3b(iii) [1] (the naming, verbatim, with the examiner's comment refusing both "Down syndrome" and "polyploidy" reproduced in full); VJC Prelim 2024 P2 Q5a(i) [1] (polyploidy read off a triploid karyotype); TJC Prelim 2023 P1 Q17, key A, and YIJC Prelim 2025 P1 Q12, key C (monosomy and trisomy against named syndromes). The figure is the school's own Fig. 16, 2.5 p. 22. Archetype: data / figure interpretation used as a deduction, at the hardest tier, the cohort scored 45.66% on the nearest published equivalent. Trap: the naming trap, and it is the one an examiner wrote a comment about. The consequence of non-disjunction is aneuploidy; "polyploidy" is refused outright and "Down syndrome" is refused unless the stem fixes which aneuploidy. Second trap: naming only the trisomic gamete, both (n+1) and (n−1) are required, and in at least one scheme that is a gateway point. Third trap: assuming all aneuploidy is meiotic, when the mosaic form is mitotic, which is Specimen P1 Q15. LOs: 2(k) chromosomal aberration, numerical, including aneuploidy as in trisomy 21. Reach-back 2(h) the centromere and its function.
